    15. Product -algebras and product measures#

    In Units 1 and 2 we constructed Lebesgue measure on in two stages. The Lebesgue outer measure assigns to a set the smallest total volume of a countable cover by rectangles, and the Carathéodory criterion then selects a -algebra, containing all Borel sets, on which this outer measure is countably additive. In the plane, the volume of a rectangle is the product of the lengths of its two sides. These notes carry out the same two-stage construction on the Cartesian product of two measure spaces and . The sides of a rectangle are now measurable sets and , and the rectangle receives the cost . The outcome is the product measure , a measure on that satisfies Product measures are the setting for iterated integrals: Tonelli’s theorem (Theorem 16.1) and Fubini’s theorem (Theorem 17.1) compute integrals with respect to by integrating first in one variable and then in the other.

    Two further questions accompany the construction. The first is its compatibility with Lebesgue measure: the product of Lebesgue measures on and on is Lebesgue measure on the Borel subsets of . The second is uniqueness: when and are -finite, is the only measure on the product -algebra that satisfies the rectangle formula above, whereas without -finiteness several such measures can exist.

    After studying these notes, you will be able to do the following.

    • Describe the product -algebra through measurable rectangles and prove that .

    • Compute the sections of sets and functions.

    • Define the product outer measure through countable covers by measurable rectangles and compute its value on rectangles.

    • Prove that product-measurable sets are Carathéodory measurable and deduce the existence of the product measure.

    • Identify the product of Lebesgue measures with Lebesgue measure on Borel sets.

    • State and prove the uniqueness of the product of -finite measures, and exhibit two different measures that agree on rectangles when -finiteness fails.

    Throughout these notes, and are measure spaces; no -finiteness is assumed until Section 15.5. Arithmetic in uses the convention (the notes 7. The Lebesgue integral of non-negative functions). With this convention, multiplication in is commutative and associative and distributes over addition.

    15.2 Sections of sets and functions#

    An iterated integral first freezes the variable and integrates the function with respect to . For the inner integral to be defined, this function must be -measurable; this is proved as part of Tonelli’s theorem (Theorem 16.1). The functions and sets obtained by freezing one variable are called sections.

    15.3 The product outer measure#

    We now follow the construction of Lebesgue outer measure. In the notes 3. Outer measures, a cost on a family of sets containing generates an outer measure , which assigns to a set the infimum of the total costs of its countable covers by members of the family. Here the family is , and the cost of a measurable rectangle is the product of the measures of its sides, This cost depends only on the set and not on the chosen sides. Indeed, a non-empty rectangle determines its sides as its images under and , and every representation of the empty set has an empty side, so its cost is by the convention .

    15.5 Maximality and uniqueness of the product measure#

    Theorem 15.9 produces one measure on that satisfies the rectangle formula. Other constructions produce measures with the same values on rectangles; for instance, Theorem 16.1 shows that is such a measure when and are -finite. This section compares all measures that satisfy the rectangle formula. The outer measure construction always yields the largest of them.
